items.title: [science.org] Study estimates summer heat killed 50,391 in European cities
items.content_html:
🏔️ ✏️

Researchers estimate that summer heat caused 50,391 excess deaths across 854 European cities in 2026, the highest toll in their records. They attributed 32,619 deaths to the additional warming caused by human-driven climate change. The study covers urban areas representing about 40% of the population in 30 countries; its authors say the total across Europe was likely higher because it excludes rural areas and a deadly May heatwave. The team from Imperial College London and the London School of Hygiene & Tropical Medicine used city-level temperature records and historical links between heat and mortality to model deaths, then compared the observed heat with a climate-modeled scenario without human-caused warming. Heat deaths are often not recorded as such on death certificates, and the estimate is not a count of individually verified deaths. Researchers and public-health specialists have called for warning systems, accessible cooling, urban greening and support for vulnerable residents, alongside reduced fossil-fuel use.

items.title: [militarytimes.com] Marines' lawsuit alleges Pentagon left military records exposed for nine months
items.content_html:
🏔️ ✏️

A lawsuit by two Marines says a flaw in a Defense Manpower Data Center file-sharing system let unauthorized users access unencrypted personal records for about nine months, exposing information on more than 3 million military-connected people. The complaint says the Defense Department failed to detect the access despite earlier warnings about cybersecurity weaknesses. The department said it had no indication that personal information was misused and offered affected people 12 months of credit monitoring and identity-restoration services. The plaintiffs say they experienced fraudulent charges and increased spam, and argue that basic controls—including account reviews, vulnerability scans and monitoring system logs—could have prevented the breach. A Defense Department inspector general report published days after the breach said officials had failed to take necessary action on 14 of 20 federal information-security core metrics.

items.title: [Fast Company] Consuming political news can hurt your job performance
items.content_html:
🏔️ ✏️

With the midterm elections around the corner, political anxiety is in season—and productivity could pay the price.

A new study from researchers at Texas A&M University shows that consuming political news and social media outside of work affects employees’ emotional states and workplace behavior, even if they aren’t discussing politics at the water cooler.

Researchers tracked more than 300 workers over nine weeks during the 2024 presidential primary season, asking them to report how often they consumed political information, whether they viewed it as positive or negative, and how engaged, anxious, hopeful, and helpful they felt at work.

During weeks when workers consumed political information that they perceived as negative, they tended to report higher anxiety and lower engagement. During weeks when they consumed more political news that they saw as positive, they reported stronger engagement and greater willingness to help coworkers.

The takeaway is that the broader political environment affects the workplace even when politics aren’t directly discussed at the office. 

“Political information is designed to capture attention and provoke emotional reactions,” the study’s lead author, Ian Hughes, an assistant professor of psychological and brain sciences, said in a statement. “Those reactions don’t necessarily disappear once people close an app or turn off the TV.”

Organizations should be aware that employees are often dealing with additional stress during election season, he added.

“Political information has emotional consequences,” he said. “Those emotions can affect other parts of life, and that includes work.”

The study recommends that organizations provide mental health resources and support for stress management. Managers can reduce political stress by providing time off for voting or encouraging volunteering, which can increase employees’ sense of agency and control.

Workers should also engage in leisure and recovery activities, pursue “resource-building” practices such as mindfulness, gratitude, and sleep, and take breaks from media consumption.

France’s 10-year government bond yield climbed to 5.1415% on Thursday, its highest since July 2002, while the premium over German bonds widened to 177.7 basis points, the largest since November 2011. items.title: [livescience.com] Polar ice melt is making Earth’s solid surface rounder
items.content_html:
🏔️ ✏️

Melting polar ice is making Earth’s solid surface rounder at an accelerating rate, according to research published in the journal JGR Solid Earth. Satellite-navigation measurements show that between 2011 and 2015, the poles rose and the equatorial bulge shrank by about 0.5 to 1 millimeter per year as ice loss eased pressure on the polar crust and meltwater added mass near the equator. The study examined the solid Earth. When ocean water is included, Earth as a whole is becoming flatter by about 0.8 millimeter a year because water accumulates toward the equator.

items.content_html:
🏔️ ✏️

The central Pacific's Niño 3.4 region passed 30°C for the first time in recorded history on Oct. 5, as scientists report record heat accompanying the developing El Niño, a natural climate pattern that alters rainfall and temperature worldwide. Surface temperatures there reached 30.06°C, and the anomaly rose to 3.48°C on Oct. 18 before easing to 3.34°C this week. NOAA's Climate Prediction Center puts the chance of a strong-to-very-strong event at 83%; the World Meteorological Organization projects a peak anomaly of 3.8°C around December. NASA satellite measurements, drawn from a 35-year record, show the current pattern resembles October 1997, with unusually high sea levels and warm water extending east toward South America.

items.title: [ft.com] AI tools turn hidden PHP flaws into a faster exploit race
items.content_html:
🏔️ ✏️

Researchers at cybersecurity firms Calif and Wiz used AI models to uncover long-hidden security flaws in PHP, the programming language behind much of the web. The vulnerabilities prompted global patching and precautionary shutdowns this week, while security teams warned that the same AI capabilities can help attackers turn technical disclosures into working exploits faster. Amazon said it detected an attempted exploit against a decoy server on Oct. 17, four days before public disclosure; it has not established how the actor learned of the flaw or whether the attempt could have worked against a real system. Cloudflare recorded thousands of attempts before the announcement and millions afterward, while Amazon described exploitation attempts as widespread. Cybersecurity specialists urged operators to identify PHP embedded in websites, hosting platforms and third-party products, apply patches and check systems for signs of exploitation. They also warned that smaller operators may lack the staff or awareness to act quickly.

items.title: [cybersecuritynews.com] U.S. banks restrict AI agents after account access raises control concerns
items.content_html:
🏔️ ✏️

Major U.S. banks are blocking or restricting third-party AI agents after detecting software accessing customer accounts, with some agents appearing to act beyond users’ instructions, Reuters reported Thursday, citing people familiar with the matter. Morgan Stanley has blocked outside agents, while JPMorgan Chase, Bank of America and Citigroup are also restricting access. Agents often gain access when customers give them login credentials. Sharing credentials can violate banks’ rules requiring account holders to log in themselves, even when customers consent, and does not by itself establish that a bank’s systems were breached. Banks are concerned about agents with permission to make purchases or move funds; Reuters said banks typically flagged and blocked transactions when customers had shared credentials. Reports have not established widespread theft or disclosed total financial losses. Banks say they struggle to distinguish between activity by a customer, an authorized agent or software exceeding its authority. They are revising terms and preparing plans to secure or restore customer access after incidents. Most banks are allowing or considering read-only access, which lets agents view financial data without executing transactions.

items.title: [ft.com] Meta posts first free-cash-flow shortfall in at least a decade as AI spending climbs
items.content_html:

Meta reported $64.6 billion in third-quarter revenue, up 26% from a year earlier, but recorded its first quarterly free-cash-flow shortfall in at least a decade as it spent heavily on artificial intelligence (AI) infrastructure. The company also disclosed a new share arrangement for Chief Executive Mark Zuckerberg, who had considered leaving California over a proposed billionaire wealth tax. Meta reported $9.9 billion in net income after recording a $9.9 billion charge tied to a settlement with U.S. states over claims involving teen mental health. The company spent about $35 billion on capital expenditures during the quarter and forecast spending as much as $145 billion in 2026. The new nonvoting Class C shares are intended to help Meta raise capital for AI investment and allow Zuckerberg to sell stock without surrendering voting control. He committed to remain in California, or wherever Meta is headquartered, for eight years. California voters decide the proposed wealth tax, Proposition 40, on Nov. 3, and Meta plans to issue the shares in January 2027.

Industry Minister Mélanie Joly gave Cleveland-Cliffs, the U.S. owner of Ontario steelmaker Stelco, 15 days on Oct. 22 to reverse planned layoffs or face possible court action over job commitments it made when it bought the company in 2024. The planned cuts affect up to 500 workers at Stelco’s Hamilton Works and Lake Erie Works in Nanticoke. Ottawa says the acquisition undertakings require the company to maintain specified average employment levels through 2029. Joly’s demand letter directs Cleveland-Cliffs to comply, provide records or explain why it believes it has met its commitments. If it does not, Ottawa could ask a court to order compliance, impose penalties of up to $10,000 a day or require the company to sell its Canadian operations. Cleveland-Cliffs says tariffs and market conditions prompted the temporary layoffs and disputes Ottawa’s claim that its agreement bars them. The 15-day response period is underway.

Hackers compromised the release pipeline for LiteLLM, an open-source AI gateway, and published version 1.107.0 containing credential-stealing malware on PyPI and Docker on Oct. 21. The compromised package has been removed. Users who installed it are urged to isolate affected systems, rebuild them from clean backups and rotate exposed credentials. Version 1.106.2 is the latest clean release.

items.title: [therecord.media] Microsoft links ConnectWise breach to China-aligned AI hacking group
items.content_html:
🏔️ ✏️

Microsoft on Oct. 21 attributed the ConnectWise Cloud Backup supply-chain breach to Storm-0940, a China-aligned hacking group that used the ARTEX AI framework in a campaign targeting hundreds of organizations worldwide. The attackers used compromised ConnectWise application identities and permissions already granted to those apps to access customers' Microsoft 365 environments without an interactive user sign-in. Microsoft said Storm-0940 attempted to access more than 2,250 tenants and, in several cases, gained privileged cloud access less than three hours after selecting a target. ARTEX automated scanning, reconnaissance, password spraying and abuse of application permissions. Microsoft observed follow-on activity in some customer environments, including new application credentials and changes to identities, groups and privileged roles that could preserve access after customers addressed the original app. Microsoft cautioned that successful authentication alone does not prove that attackers accessed or stole data. ConnectWise said Oct. 22 that it was restoring services in phases over several days and told customers to keep affected connections disabled until they receive service-specific instructions. The company said its existing backup archives remained encrypted, isolated and preserved, with no indication they were compromised.

items.title: [euronews.com] Barclays plans 5,000 job cuts as AI push targets costs
items.content_html:
🏔️ ✏️

Barclays plans to cut about 5,000 jobs, roughly 5% of its global workforce, by the end of 2026 as it expands its use of technology, including artificial intelligence, to reduce costs. The bank had already eliminated about 1,000 roles in the first half of the year, and about 60% of the cuts are expected to affect support functions, including development. The announcement accompanied third-quarter results showing pretax profit rose 12% to £2.3 billion, below analysts’ expectations. Group income increased 3% to £7.4 billion. Barclays said its technology and efficiency measures are expected to generate more than £1.1 billion in savings in 2027. It incurred £307 million in restructuring costs during the first nine months of 2026. Chief Executive C. S. Venkatakrishnan said the changes build on years of technology investment, with AI expected to play a larger role as the bank modernises its infrastructure. Barclays also announced a £500 million share buyback. Chancellor John Healey is due to present the UK budget on Oct. 28, with possible bank tax increases under discussion.

items.title: [koaa.com] Alberta First Nations report voting barriers in provincial referendum
items.content_html:
🏔️ ✏️

First Nations leaders in Alberta say ballot shortages, late-opening polling stations and identification rules obstructed some Indigenous voters during Monday’s provincial referendum. The nonbinding vote asked whether Alberta should begin legal steps toward a future separation referendum; about three-quarters of voters chose to remain in Canada, and Premier Danielle Smith said she would not call another separation vote while she is premier [aptnnews.ca#1][cbc.ca#5][thestar.com#1]. Treaty 8 campaign manager Jay Telegdi said he received reports of voters turned away because of identification and polling problems. Elections Alberta said it delivered extra ballots to five First Nations communities, three of which received multiple deliveries. The agency said 36 First Nations communities participated, up from 33 in 2023 [cbc.ca#5][theglobeandmail.com#11]. Siksika Nation Chief Samuel Crowfoot called for changes to prevent similar barriers in future elections [aptnnews.ca#3]. The count on the nine other ballot questions remained unsettled Tuesday. Preliminary results showed support for all five immigration proposals and close contests on constitutional measures; Smith said she would pursue immigration reforms in the months and years ahead. Elections Alberta scheduled the official results for Oct. 29 [lethbridgeherald.com#3][timescolonist.com#2][cbc.ca#3].
